name: Nathang Valley
tagline: A high yak valley where the 1888 campaign was decided
meta_description: Nathang (Gnathang) Valley on the Silk Route, about 3,750 m: yak meadows, the 1888 war memorial, homestays, permits for Indians, altitude tips and costs.
summary: Nathang (Gnathang) Valley is a wide high valley at about 3,750 m on the Silk Route in Pakyong district, with a small village, a gumpa, yak pastures and army camps. In May 1888 Tibetan forces attacked the British camp here. Indian nationals only; sleep at Zuluk first and come up acclimatised.
intro: Nathang is the open space at the top of the Silk Route. After the forest and loops below Zuluk, the road crosses the Lungthung ridge and drops onto a broad valley floor of grass, streams and grazing yaks, surrounded by bare ridges. Gnathang village itself is tiny: the 2011 census counted 13 households and 60 people. There is a gumpa, Gnathang Gadenchoeling, a Krishna temple and a few homestays, set among army camps.

Survey data place the valley floor at about 3,700–3,800 m; travel sites often quote 13,500 ft. Either way it is high, and nights are bitterly cold. The valley turns gold in October and November, is often snowbound from December to March, and greens up with wild flowers from May. From a ridge nearby, the Doklam plateau is visible on a clear day, about 35 km away.

Most visitors pass through on the Silk Route circuit, stopping at the war memorial and gumpa before continuing to Kupup and Tsomgo or back down to Zuluk. Hardy, acclimatised travellers spend a night. Indian nationals only, with the Silk Route permit arranged via Rongli. Snow and army movements can close the road. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: 22 May 1888: the attack on the Gnathang camp
story.text: After taking the Tibetan fort at Lingtu in March 1888, Brigadier-General Thomas Graham's force set up defences at Gnathang, a plateau three or four miles north of the fort. The Tibetans, far from withdrawing, gathered reinforcements beyond the passes. According to Wikipedia's account of the Sikkim expedition, at 7 am on 22 May they attacked the British defences with what British reports claimed were 3,000 men. Fighting lasted until about 10 am. The British lost three killed and eight wounded, and claimed to have killed around a hundred Tibetans. Later that year Graham's men drove the Tibetans back over Tuko La and Jelep La. The British held Gnathang through 1889 and 1890, and Wikipedia notes a war memorial here to the men who lost their lives during that occupation. The settlement the soldiers left behind became the herding village you see today.
story.source: Wikipedia: Sikkim expedition; Wikipedia: Nathang Valley

little_known.fact: The 2011 census recorded Gnathang village as just 13 households and 60 people on 16 hectares, making it one of the smallest permanent settlements on the Silk Route.
Nathang's yaks are reared not only for milk and meat; Wikipedia notes they have been used to carry loads for border road construction, including roads towards Doka La.
On 22 May 1888 Tibetan forces attacked the British camp at Gnathang from 7 am to about 10 am; the British reported three killed and eight wounded.

facts: Oct–Nov for gold grass and clear skies; Apr–May for flowers
≈ 115 km · 5.5–6 h via Rongli and Zuluk; ≈ 75 km · 3–3.5 h via Tsomgo and Kupup
Yak meadows, 1888 war memorial, winter snow
Silk Route permit via Rongli; Indian nationals only

highlights.title: The war memorial
highlights.text: A small memorial near Gnathang remembers men who died during the British occupation of the valley after the 1888 campaign. It is a short stop, and a good place to piece together the story of Jeluk, Lingtu and Gnathang.

highlights.title: Yaks on the valley floor
highlights.text: Herding families graze yaks on the open meadows. Stop the car, keep your distance and watch: yaks are calm but large, and the herders' dogs are protective. In winter the herds move lower.

highlights.title: Gnathang Gadenchoeling Gumpa
highlights.text: The village gumpa is a small, working Buddhist temple for the herding families. Walk round clockwise, ask before entering, and leave a small offering if you wish.

highlights.title: Gold in October, white in January
highlights.text: In October and November the valley grass turns gold under deep blue skies. From December to March it is often under snow, beautiful and unpredictable; roads close at short notice.

highlights.title: The road to Kupup
highlights.text: From Nathang the road climbs to Kupup at about 3,940 m, past the Old Baba Mandir shrine, Elephant Lake and the Yak golf course, before dropping towards Tsomgo and Gangtok.

how_to_reach.text: No shared jeeps serve Nathang for tourists. Shared SUV seats on Silk Route group tours from Gangtok or Siliguri are the budget option; otherwise hire a permit-registered vehicle from Rongli or Gangtok.

From Zuluk, about 25 km and 1–1.5 hours via Thambi and Lungthung. From Gangtok via Rongli and Zuluk, about 115 km and 5.5–6 hours; the shorter road via Tsomgo and Kupup is usually used for the return to Gangtok. Sikkim-registered vehicles only.

Not in one day. Drive to Aritar, Padamchen or Zuluk first (5–7 hours via Rangpo, or via Kalimpong and Rhenock when NH10 is shut after monsoon slides), then come up to Nathang next day. Check current status before you travel.

costs: Shared SUV seat on a 3-day Silk Route tour
where_to_stay: Gnathang has a few family homestays with basic rooms, kitchen stoves and simple meals included; expect frost, shared or indoor toilets and water that may freeze overnight. We use them only for travellers who have already slept at Zuluk or Padamchen. Most of our guests visit Nathang by day and sleep at Zuluk, 1–1.5 hours below, or at Lungthung if acclimatised. For comfort after the high road, Gangtok is about 3–3.5 hours away via Kupup and Tsomgo.
tips: Never come to Nathang straight from Gangtok or the plains to sleep; spend a night at Zuluk first.
Keep walks short and slow; even 100 m uphill feels hard at this height.
Pack a down jacket, thermals, gloves and a warm cap in every season.
Keep your distance from yaks and herd dogs, and ask herders before photographing them.
Carry cash and snacks; there is no ATM and very little to buy.

experiences.title: Visit the Nathang war memorial
experiences.best_time: Morning, Oct–May when the road is open
experiences.summary: A short stop at the memorial near Gnathang that remembers men who died during the British occupation of the valley after the 1888 campaign, with the battlefield of 22 May 1888 around you.
body: The memorial is small and plain, and many tour vehicles stop for only a few minutes. Give it longer. Wikipedia's article on Nathang Valley notes it remembers the men who lost their lives during the occupation of Gnathang in 1889 and 1890, the period when British Indian troops held the valley after driving Tibetan forces out in 1888.

Stand with your back to the memorial and the whole campaign is laid out: Lingtu ridge to the south, where the Tibetan fort stood; the valley floor where the British camp was attacked at 7 am on 22 May 1888; and the passes to the north and east, Tuko La and Jelep La, which Graham's force crossed later that year.

Many of those who died in such campaigns died of cold and disease, not only in battle. Be respectful: do not climb on the memorial. It sits near army areas, so ask before photographing and follow any instructions from soldiers. Indian nationals only, with the Silk Route permit.

faqs.q: What does the Nathang war memorial commemorate?
faqs.a: According to Wikipedia's article on Nathang Valley, it remembers men who lost their lives during the British occupation of Gnathang in 1889–1890, following the 1888 Sikkim expedition against Tibetan forces. The valley was the scene of a Tibetan attack on the British camp on 22 May 1888.

faqs.q: How long should we spend at the memorial?
faqs.a: Twenty to forty-five minutes is enough to see the memorial, look over the battlefield and take in the story. Combine it with Gnathang's gumpa and a tea stop. At this altitude, walk slowly and keep the stop short if anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: Can we photograph the memorial?
faqs.a: Usually yes, but the memorial is close to army areas where photography may be restricted. Ask soldiers if you are unsure, keep army posts and vehicles out of your frame, and never fly a drone. Respect the site as a grave memorial, not a photo prop.

experiences.title: Slow walk across the yak meadows
experiences.summary: A gentle, flat walk on the valley floor near Gnathang, among grazing yaks, streams and wild flowers in season. Easy on paper, slow in practice at 3,750 m, and the best way to feel the scale of the valley.
body: The valley floor is wide and mostly flat, which makes it the one place on the upper Silk Route where you can walk without climbing. Start from the village, follow the tracks along the stream, and you are soon among grazing yaks with the bare ridges all around. In May and June small wild flowers appear in the grass; in October the meadows turn gold.

Herding families have used these pastures for generations, and the yaks are their livelihood. Keep at least 15–20 m from the animals, never walk between a mother and calf, and give herd dogs a wide berth. Ask herders before taking photographs; many are happy to chat if you have time.

Even on the flat, the altitude slows you. Walk at half your normal pace, drink water and turn back if you feel headache or dizziness. Wind picks up after midday, so go in the late morning. Stay away from army fences and do not cross into marked areas.

faqs.q: Are the yaks at Nathang dangerous?
faqs.a: Yaks are generally calm, but they are large, horned animals and can charge if they feel threatened, especially mothers with calves. Keep 15–20 m away, do not feed or touch them, and give herd dogs space. Follow the herders' signals; they know their animals.

faqs.q: When is the Nathang Valley green?
faqs.a: From about May to September the grass is green and flowers appear, but June to September is monsoon season, when roads are risky and clouds sit low. Late May and early June are a good compromise. October and November bring the golden-brown look many photographs show.

faqs.q: Is walking at Nathang hard?
faqs.a: The ground is easy, the air is thin. At about 3,750 m most people walk slowly and stop often. Keep walks short, go at your own pace and turn back at the first sign of headache, dizziness or breathlessness at rest. Children and seniors should take it especially gently.

experiences.title: Butter lamps at the Gnathang gumpa
experiences.summary: A quiet visit to Gnathang Gadenchoeling Gumpa, the small Buddhist temple of the valley's herding families. Prayer wheels, flags snapping in the wind and, if the caretaker is in, the chance to light a butter lamp.
body: Gnathang Gadenchoeling is a village gumpa, not a grand monastery, and that is its charm. It serves the families who live in the valley year round, and it is often quiet, with only the wind in the prayer flags. If the caretaker is there, you may be allowed inside to see the altar and light a butter lamp.

Walk round the building clockwise, turning the prayer wheels with your right hand. Remove shoes before entering, keep voices low, and do not point your feet at the altar if you sit. Ask before photographing inside; some caretakers allow it, others do not. A small offering at the altar is welcome but never expected.

Combine the gumpa with the war memorial and a walk on the meadows. In winter the gumpa may be locked when families move lower. Wikipedia also lists a Krishna temple in the village, a sign of the mix of faiths on the Silk Route.

faqs.q: Is Gnathang Gadenchoeling Gumpa open to visitors?
faqs.a: Usually, during the day when the caretaker is around. It is a small village gumpa, so hours are informal. If it is locked, you can still walk round the outside and its prayer wheels. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering, and ask before photographing inside.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists visit the gumpa?
faqs.a: Yes. Visitors of any faith are welcome if they are respectful. Walk clockwise around the building, keep quiet inside, and follow any guidance from the caretaker. Making an offering is a personal choice; a few rupees or a butter lamp are customary for those who wish.

faqs.q: Are there festivals at the Gnathang gumpa?
faqs.a: Losar, the Tibetan new year in February or March, and other Buddhist days are observed by the village, but the road may be snowbound at that time and celebrations are small and private. We do not promise any public event. Ask us before planning a trip around a date.

experiences.title: See the valley under winter snow
experiences.best_time: Late Dec–Feb, when the road is open
experiences.cost: Included in Silk Route car; gumboots ≈ ₹100–200 if available
experiences.summary: From late December to February, Nathang Valley often lies under deep snow, and the drive over Lungthung becomes a white road between drifts. Spectacular when it works; plan spare days because it often does not.
body: Snow transforms Nathang. The valley floor, the ridges and the village roofs turn white, the streams freeze at the edges, and the yaks stand out dark against the snow. For many Indian travellers this is the most dramatic snow scene they can reach by road in the Eastern Himalaya.

Getting here in winter depends on the road. After heavy snowfall, the army and road teams may stop vehicles at Zuluk or Lungthung until the road is cleared, and permits are sometimes paused. Black ice is common in the mornings. We plan winter Silk Route trips with at least one spare day, check with Nathang homestays each evening, and follow drivers' calls without argument.

Dress for serious cold, well below freezing even at noon in the shade: down jacket, thermals, waterproof boots, gloves, cap and sunglasses against the glare. Keep children's time in the snow short. Sleep at Zuluk rather than Nathang in deep winter unless you are experienced. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Nathang Valley open in winter?
faqs.a: Often, but closures after heavy snowfall are common between December and March, sometimes for several days. Permits may be paused when the road is unsafe. We confirm each evening with homestays and drivers and keep spare days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How cold is Nathang in January?
faqs.a: Very cold: night temperatures can fall to minus 10 to minus 20 °C, and days often stay below freezing in the shade, with strong wind. Water pipes freeze. Only stay overnight in winter if you are well equipped and acclimatised; most of our guests visit by day from Zuluk.

faqs.q: Can we drive back to Gangtok via Kupup in winter?
faqs.a: Sometimes. The road from Nathang to Kupup and Tsomgo is higher and can close after snow even when the Zuluk side is open. If it is shut, you return to Gangtok the way you came, via Zuluk and Rongli, which takes longer. Plan for both and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Nathang Valley?
faqs.a: Survey elevation data put Gnathang village at about 3,700–3,800 m; travel sites often quote 13,500 ft (about 4,100 m). Either way, it is the highest overnight stop on the Silk Route for most travellers, so acclimatise at Zuluk or Padamchen first and keep exertion low.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay overnight at Nathang?
faqs.a: For healthy, acclimatised adults, generally yes. Sleep at Zuluk or Padamchen the night before, drink water, avoid alcohol and walk slowly. Headache, nausea, dizziness or breathlessness at rest mean you should go down. Infants, and people with heart or lung conditions, should not sleep at Nathang.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Nathang Valley?
faqs.a: No. Nathang is on the restricted upper Silk Route, open to Indian nationals only with a permit arranged via Rongli. Foreign travellers are not allowed beyond the lower villages. Rules change from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Nathang or Zuluk: where should we stay?
faqs.a: Zuluk for most people: it is about 1,000 m lower, warmer and has more homestays. Choose Nathang only if you are acclimatised, want a night in a high valley and accept basic, very cold rooms. Many of our guests sleep at Zuluk and visit Nathang by day on the way to Kupup.

faqs.q: How do we get from Nathang to Gangtok?
faqs.a: The shortest road is via Kupup, Baba Mandir and Tsomgo Lake, about 75 km and 3–3.5 hours, when it is open. The alternative is back via Zuluk and Rongli, about 115 km and 5.5–6 hours. Your permit and driver decide which is possible that day; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is there to see at Nathang?
faqs.a: The war memorial to men who died during the 1888–1890 British occupation, Gnathang Gadenchoeling Gumpa, yak pastures, and the open valley itself. The drive on to Kupup passes the Old Baba Mandir shrine and Elephant Lake. Expect a quiet, open landscape rather than built sights.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Nathang Valley?
faqs.a: October and November for clear skies and gold grass; April and May for milder days and the first green; late December to February for snow, with closure risk. Avoid June to September, when monsoon slides cut the Silk Route road and clouds hide the views.

faqs.q: Is there electricity and mobile signal at Nathang?
faqs.a: Homestays have electricity, though cuts are common, and some keep a backup. Mobile signal is weak and operator-dependent; many guests have no data at all. Carry a power bank, keep devices warm, download offline maps and tell family you may be out of touch.

faqs.q: What should we pack for Nathang?
faqs.a: Down or padded jacket, thermals, fleece, warm cap, gloves, two pairs of thick socks, sturdy shoes or boots, sunglasses, sunscreen, lip balm, a refillable bottle, a torch, basic medicines and photo ID with photocopies for permit checks. Bring snacks; shops are few.
